title: Self-hosting DeskcommCRM: pin the stable channel, and keep WAHA off the public internet
summary:
This is a third-party deployment note, not official DeskcommCRM documentation. It follows GitHub release v1.100.0 (published 2026-11-04, checked on 2026-11-05 09:30 Asia/Shanghai). The project is licensed under MIT. Official materials start at https://github.com/melgarafael/DeskcommCRM. Recheck the current release, and the WAHA image pin, before you install or upgrade.

The main path is the official hostgator-setup-kit/install.sh on a VPS you already control. You do not need to compile the app on the server. Production Compose publishes only Caddy on TCP 80 and 443. The app, worker, scheduler, Redis, and WAHA stay on the internal network. Do not publish a WAHA dashboard, Redis, or an application admin port. The production file also leaves the WAHA dashboard disabled by default; do not open it to the internet for convenience. Recommended memory is about 4 GB. A 2 GB machine may start, but it is a tight limit once WhatsApp sessions are in use.

Pin the app, worker, and scheduler to the same release channel. In this stack, :stable means the latest complete release, not the default-branch tip. :latest follows that tip and can include unpublished code. A historical mismatch was an updated web UI with a worker still built from an older or unpublished image; keep the three services on the same channel. For the database, use the Supabase Session pooler URI, not a direct or IPv6-only connection. Do not treat supabase db push as the self-hosted schema path: early migration files may be stubs, and the real schema is in supabase/baseline.sql. The installer and updater apply that baseline; a “successful” push can still leave an empty database. On ARM, use the official ARM WAHA image and do not force an amd64 platform flag. A full Chinese step-by-step guide (installer path, Compose boundaries, WhatsApp channels, backups and rollback) is here: https://9012938178391.gumroad.com/l/xyobnn

title: git push --force-with-lease Still Deleted a Commit: Blame Auto-Fetch
summary:
I squashed two commits, typed git push --force-with-lease, and felt responsible. That's the safe force push. Everyone says so. I'd even told a junior dev to alias it.

Ten minutes later a teammate asked where their commit went.

It was gone from main on the remote. My "safe" push had overwritten it, and Git didn't print a single warning. The culprit wasn't me, and it wasn't Git being buggy. It was my editor running git fetch in the background while I was rebasing.

This post shows exactly why git push --force-with-lease fails when something fetches behind your back, gives you a 30-second script that reproduces it, and shows the one flag that closes the hole.

TL;DR

  • git push --force-with-lease with no argument compares the remote branch against your local remote-tracking ref (origin/main), not against what you actually rebased on.
  • Any git fetch after you started rewriting (editor auto-fetch, a GUI client, a script, a coding agent "checking upstream") updates origin/main silently. The lease now matches, and your push overwrites the new commits.
  • Fix: add --force-if-includes (Git 2.30+), or set git config --global push.useForceIfIncludes true. It rejects the push unless the remote tip actually appears in your local branch's reflog.
  • Bulletproof alternative: pin the expected SHA yourself with --force-with-lease=main:.

What does git push --force-with-lease actually check?

--force-with-lease checks one thing: "is the branch on the remote still pointing at the commit I think it points at?" If yes, the force push goes through. If no, it's rejected with (stale info).

The catch is where "what I think" comes from. When you don't pass an explicit value, Git uses your remote-tracking ref. For main, that's refs/remotes/origin/main, the thing you see as origin/main in git log.

That ref is not a snapshot of what you based your work on. It's a cache that gets overwritten by every git fetch. Every one. Including the ones you didn't run.

So the protection boils down to this:

Event origin/main (local) main (on remote) Lease result
You start a rebase B B -
Teammate pushes C B C would reject
Background fetch runs C C passes
You force push C your rewrite C is gone

The lease is supposed to answer "did anyone push since I looked?" After a background fetch, it answers "did anyone push since the last time anything on my machine looked?" Those are very different questions.

How do I reproduce the force-with-lease overwrite?

Paste this into a terminal. It uses a local bare repo as the "remote", so it touches nothing real.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
rm -rf /tmp/lease && mkdir /tmp/lease && cd /tmp/lease

git init -q --bare -b main origin.git

# Me: two commits, pushed
git init -q -b main me && cd me
git remote add origin ../origin.git
echo one > f && git add f && git commit -qm "A"
echo two >> f && git commit -qam "B"
git push -q -u origin main
cd ..

# Teammate clones
git clone -q origin.git teammate

# I start rewriting history: squash B into A
cd me
git reset -q --soft HEAD~1
git commit -q --amend -m "A+B squashed"
cd ..

# Teammate pushes on top of B
cd teammate
echo three >> f && git commit -qam "C (teammate)"
git push -q origin main
cd ..

# My editor auto-fetches in the background
cd me
git fetch -q origin

# I push "safely"
git push --force-with-lease origin main
git log --oneline origin/main

The push prints (forced update). The log shows one commit: A+B squashed. Commit C, the teammate's work, is no longer reachable from main on the remote.

Now delete the git fetch -q origin line and run it again. The push gets rejected with (stale info), exactly like the docs promise. One fetch is the entire difference between "safe" and "silently destructive."

What runs git fetch behind my back?

More things than you'd guess. In my case it was editor auto-fetch, but anything that updates remote-tracking refs counts:

  1. Editor auto-fetch. VS Code has a git.autofetch setting. Plenty of people turn it on so the sync badge stays fresh. Other IDEs and Git GUIs have their own periodic fetch.
  2. Desktop Git clients. Several fetch on a timer so they can show "3 commits behind."
  3. Shell prompts. Some fancy prompt setups fetch to show ahead/behind counts.
  4. Coding agents. If you let an agent run git fetch to "see what changed upstream" while you're mid-rebase in the same repo, it's the same problem with extra steps.
  5. You, in another terminal. git fetch updates all remote-tracking branches, not just the one you're thinking about. Fetching to check out a coworker's PR branch also refreshes origin/main.

None of these do anything wrong. They're doing their job. The flaw is that a plain --force-with-lease treats "my machine has seen it" as "I have integrated it."

How does --force-if-includes fix force-with-lease?

--force-if-includes adds a second check: the current tip of the remote-tracking ref must be reachable from somewhere in your local branch's reflog. In plain English: you must have actually had that commit in your branch at some point, by pulling, rebasing onto it, or merging it.

A background fetch updates origin/main, but it never touches your local main reflog. So commit C was fetched but never integrated, and the push gets rejected.

Change the last push in the script to:

git push --force-with-lease --force-if-includes origin main

You get:

 ! [rejected]        main -> main (remote ref updated since checkout)

That's the message you wanted the first time. Now git pull --rebase, look at C, put it on top of your squash, and push again. This time the check passes, because C is in your history.

Make it permanent so you never have to remember:

git config --global push.useForceIfIncludes true

With that set, every --force-with-lease push also does the reflog check. It needs Git 2.30 or newer; check with git --version.

When does --force-if-includes still let a bad push through?

It's a big improvement, not magic. Know the gaps:

  • Your reflog can lie on your behalf. If you ran git reset --hard origin/main after the fetch and then reset back to your rewrite, C was in your branch's reflog for a moment. The check passes. You "integrated" it for three seconds and then threw it away.
  • It only applies to the implicit lease. If you pass an explicit expected value like --force-with-lease=main:, Git trusts your SHA and skips the reflog check. That's fine, because you're being explicit.
  • Plain --force ignores all of this. git push -f doesn't check leases at all. If muscle memory types -f, no config saves you.
  • Expired reflogs. Reflog entries expire (90 days by default for reachable entries). Not a problem for a branch you rebased this morning, but worth knowing.

What's the most bulletproof way to force push?

Pin the SHA yourself. Record what the remote looked like before you started rewriting, then pass it explicitly:

base=$(git rev-parse origin/main)   # right before you rebase
git rebase -i "$base"
# ...edit, squash, reword...
git push --force-with-lease=main:"$base" origin main

Now no background process can move the goalposts. Your expected value is a shell variable, not a ref that gets rewritten by every fetch. If the remote moved off $base for any reason, the push is rejected.

It's more typing, so I use it for shared branches and the config flag for everything else.

My setup now

Three lines in my global config, and I stopped worrying about it:

git config --global push.useForceIfIncludes true
git config --global alias.pushf 'push --force-with-lease'
git config --global alias.pf '!echo "use git pushf" && false'

The last alias is mild self-defense: if I type git pf expecting a force push, it refuses and reminds me of the safe one. I also block --force to main with branch protection on the server side, because client-side habits are only as good as the tired version of me at 6 p.m.

I left editor auto-fetch on. It's genuinely useful. It just shouldn't be able to disarm my safety check, and with --force-if-includes it can't.

So why did git push --force-with-lease delete the commit?

git push --force-with-lease deleted the commit because, without an explicit value, it only checks that the remote branch still matches your local remote-tracking ref (origin/main). A background git fetch from an editor, Git client, prompt, script or coding agent updates that ref to include your teammate's new commit, so the lease matches and the force push overwrites work you never saw. Add --force-if-includes (or set push.useForceIfIncludes true, Git 2.30+) so the push is rejected unless the remote tip is in your local branch's reflog, or pin the expected SHA with --force-with-lease=main: for a check no fetch can change.

title: Audit SPF, DMARC and SSL for a list of domains in one run
summary:
Disclosure: I build the Domain Health Audit actor mentioned below. The checks themselves are plain DNS and HTTPS, and you can do them with any tool.

If you manage many domains (an agency, an IT shop, a cold-email team), the same few problems repeat: a second SPF record, a DMARC policy stuck on p=none, a certificate about to expire, missing security headers.

What to check, and what the results mean

  • SPF: exactly one v=spf1 record. Two records is a permanent error. Check it ends in ~all or -all, and count DNS lookups (the limit is 10, includes and redirects count).
  • DMARC: a record at _dmarc.. p=none only monitors. quarantine or reject enforces. Subdomains inherit the parent's policy unless they set their own, so do not flag a subdomain as missing DMARC when the parent has it.
  • DKIM: be careful. The selector name is private, so you cannot prove DKIM is missing from outside. A good tool says "not detected for common selectors", not "missing".
  • MX: present, and pointing to the provider you expect.
  • SSL: days until expiry, invalid or self-signed certificates.
  • Security headers: HSTS, CSP, X-Frame-Options, nosniff, Referrer-Policy, and a security.txt file.

Do it from the command line 

dig +short TXT example.com | grep spf1
dig +short TXT _dmarc.example.com
echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -enddate

Fine for one domain. For fifty it gets tedious.

Doing a list

Domain Health Audit takes a list of domains and returns, for each, a 0-100 score, an A-F grade and a fix list sorted by impact, as JSON, CSV or a readable report. I cross-checked it against dig on 52 domains and found no DMARC mismatches, and DKIM never changes the score because it cannot be verified from outside. Price is $0.002 per domain, and the Apify free credit covers a trial.

For ongoing watching, Domain Change Monitor re-checks DNS, certificates and expiry on a schedule and flags what changed since the last run.

Run the audit before a client onboarding and again each quarter. Most findings are quick fixes.

If you would rather have it done for you: I offer a $15 audit report for up to 10 domains (48h): Domain Email-Security and Expiry Audit Report. There is also a fix plan with copy-paste records. I make both (LightData Tools).

title: From Monitoring Alerts to IT Actions: A Practical Guide to Closing the Loop
summary:
A monitoring alert is only useful if it changes what someone does next.

A dashboard can show a full fleet's CPU, disk, and security events and still leave an operator with the same question: "What should I do about this?" The gap isn't a lack of data. It's the missing path from signal to decision.

We think monitoring should be designed around that path. In this article, we'll turn a few common signals into practical, testable actions - and show how to avoid building an alert system that creates more work than it removes.

Start with the decision, not the metric

A metric is not actionable just because it crosses a threshold. "Disk usage is 85%" is a fact. It doesn't say whether the disk is filling steadily, whether a temporary job caused the spike, or who should respond.

Before adding a monitor, write down the decision it should support:

  • What condition is the monitor detecting?
  • What user or service impact could follow?
  • Who owns the response?
  • What is the first safe action?
  • When should the issue be escalated?

If the team can't answer those questions, keep collecting the metric, but don't page on it yet. An unowned alert is a notification with nowhere to go.

Turn a threshold into context

Thresholds are useful for catching immediate risk. Trends are what help distinguish an incident from normal variation.

For example, 85% disk use can mean very different things:

  • A stable volume has been at 85% for months and has enough headroom.
  • A volume has moved from 70% to 85% in a week.
  • A volume grew 2% in the last hour and is still climbing.

The same point-in-time value calls for different responses. Add rate of change, a comparison window, or a known operating baseline where it changes the decision.

A simple rule can estimate time to exhaustion from recent measurements. This Python example assumes the readings are evenly spaced and expressed as percentages:

from collections import deque
from statistics import mean

# (minutes since start, disk usage percent)
readings = deque([
    (0, 72.0),
    (60, 73.0),
    (120, 75.0),
    (180, 78.0),
], maxlen=12)

def estimate_minutes_to_full(samples, limit=95.0):
    if len(samples) < 2:
        return None

    elapsed = samples[-1][0] - samples[0][0]
    if elapsed <= 0:
        return None

    # Percentage points per minute, averaged across the window.
    rate = (samples[-1][1] - samples[0][1]) / elapsed
    if rate <= 0:
        return None

    remaining = limit - samples[-1][1]
    return max(0, round(remaining / rate))

minutes = estimate_minutes_to_full(readings)
if minutes is not None and minutes < 24 * 60:
    print(f"Investigate disk growth: estimated {minutes} minutes to 95%")

This is a starting point, not a forecasting system. A short window can overreact to a backup or deployment, while a long window can hide a sudden change. In production, calculate on a rolling window, account for missing samples, and make the threshold depend on the volume's role.

Give every alert an owner and a first move

An alert should carry enough information to begin triage without a second round of detective work. At minimum, include the affected host or service, the observed value, the time window, severity, owner, and a runbook or first check.

For instance, this configuration describes a monitor in terms of response, not just measurement:

name: disk-growth-risk
scope: customer-host
condition:
  metric: disk.used_percent
  above: 80
  duration: 15m
  trend:
    minimum_growth_percent_per_hour: 1.5
severity: warning
owner: platform-operations
summary: "Disk usage is high and growing on {{ host }}"
first_action: "Check largest directories and recent scheduled jobs"
runbook: "https://docs.example.net/runbooks/disk-growth"
maintenance_silence: true

title: NFS2ROOT on CentOS 7: the stock kernel is affected and gets no fix
summary:
NFS2ROOT (CVE-2026-99362) is a pre-authentication heap overflow in the Linux kernel's NFS server. A client that can reach TCP 2049 shrinks its NFSv4.1 session reply cache to zero bytes, pads a SEQUENCE request, and nfsd copies the whole reply into the empty slot buffer. No account or export access is needed. The kernel.org CNA rates it CVSS 9.8, Red Hat rates it Critical.

On CentOS 7 it reaches every NFS server running the defaults:

  • Stock 3.10: affected, per Red Hat, and the CentOS 7 source carries the same unbounded copy. nfsd serves +4.1 +4.2 out of the box, and having no exports does not help: the overflow happens during session setup. CentOS 7 gets no kernel updates.
  • ELRepo kernel-lt 5.4.278 and kernel-ml 6.9.7: inside the affected range (3.16 and later), and both lines ended without a fix.
  • CentOS 8: RHEL 8 got the fix on 2026-11-26 (4.18.0-553.190.1.el8_10), CentOS 8 did not. AlmaLinux 8, Rocky 8 and Oracle Linux 8 already ship that kernel, so converting in place is the free way out.

The fix

Disclosure: I maintain this package. GetPageSpeed's kernel-lt has carried the fix since 6.18.62-1, published on 2026-11-07, twelve days before the CVE went public. It uses the same package name as ELRepo, installs beside your current kernel, and is free for any use:

yum -y install https://extras.getpagespeed.com/release-latest.rpm
yum -y install yum-utils
yum-config-manager --enable getpagespeed-extras-corecare
yum -y install kernel-lt
grub2-set-default 0
grubby --default-kernel
reboot

Already on our 6.18 kernel but older than 6.18.62? yum -y update 'kernel-lt*', then check grubby --default-kernel before you reboot: builds before 6.18.62-2 did not move the GRUB default on update. uname -r after the reboot is the check that counts, not rpm -q.

The exposure checks, Red Hat's stopgap (stop nfs-server or firewall 2049) and the rollback are in the full write-up.

title: Replacing LocalStack with Floci 2.4.0: pin the image, and set the hostname for other containers
summary:
This is a third-party deployment note, not official Floci documentation. It follows release 2.4.0 (published 2026-10-31, checked on 2026-11-05, Asia/Shanghai). Official docs start at https://floci.io/floci/ and the LocalStack migration page is at https://floci.io/floci/getting-started/migrate-from-localstack/. Pin floci/floci:2.4.0 in production or CI; latest is only a convenience tag. If init scripts need a container-local AWS CLI or boto3, use the 2.4.0-compat image instead. The older third-party name hectorvent/floci is unmaintained; switch to floci/floci.

Floci is a local AWS emulator. It uses port 4566 and the same documented placeholder credentials as common LocalStack examples, so many SDK and CLI clients only need a new endpoint. It is not a public multi-tenant stand-in for AWS. Do not publish 4566 to the internet. For a drop-in Compose swap, changing the image and the data volume is usually enough: keep port 4566, keep the placeholder credentials, keep init files on the old LocalStack-compatible path if you already have them, and mount data at /app/data instead of /var/lib/localstack. A LocalStack-style PERSISTENCE=1 setting can be translated automatically, but only if that volume path is correct. Explicit FLOCI_* variables win over the compatibility translation.

The most common breakage is multi-container networking. Generated URLs often contain localhost. An application in another container that calls localhost:4566 is calling itself, not Floci. Set FLOCI_HOSTNAME to the Compose service name, and point the application at http://:4566. That affects queue URLs, callback URLs, and other derived endpoints. For S3 clients, prefer path-style addressing. This note does not invent performance comparisons with LocalStack. A full Chinese step-by-step guide (Compose, persistence, LocalStack swap, and CI pitfalls) is here: https://9012938178391.gumroad.com/l/zkttzt

title: Gemini 3.8 Live turns voice agents into continuity systems
summary:
TL;DR

Google’s September 15 announcement introduces Gemini 3.8 Live and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking as near-real-time reasoning models for more natural voice interaction. The announcement highlights interruptions, language switching, real-time visual context, background tools and API calls, and an Extended Thinking mode that can keep the dialogue moving while it works through a complex task. Google attributes benchmark results including 82.6 on Artificial Analysis’ Speech to Speech Quality Index, 68.6% on τ-Voice, 35.1% on Sierra’s τ-Voice-banking benchmark and 97.7% on Big Bench Audio to the Extended Thinking model. Our position is narrower and less celebratory: fluent continuity changes the reliability problem. A voice agent that never visibly “stops” can also hide when it misunderstood, delegated work, changed state or resumed with stale context. Observability has to follow the conversation, not just the final answer.

Google is selling two related capabilities. Gemini 3.8 Live is described as the scalable, cost-efficient option, combining conversational intelligence, fluid dialogue and visual grounding. Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking targets high-complexity, multi-step work. Both are presented as useful foundations for production voice agents, and Google says they are available across the Gemini app, Google Workspace and Search.

Google says these models are available to developers through the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, with Gemini Enterprise in private preview. For everyone, the announcement names Search Live; it also lists Workspace surfaces including Docs, Gmail and Keep. That breadth matters because each surface can expose a different boundary between a spoken request and an external action.

Figure: official Google visual from the Gemini 3.8 Live announcement.

The useful breakthrough is not “voice”; it is negotiated continuity

A conventional voice assistant often makes its state visible through turns: the user speaks, the system transcribes, the model answers, and the exchange ends. Gemini 3.8 Live is framed around a less tidy interaction. The user can interrupt. The conversation can switch languages. Visual context can become part of the exchange. The agent can keep a task moving in the background instead of forcing the user to wait in silence.

This is closer to collaboration than question answering. It is also harder to specify. An interruption can be a correction, a new instruction or a side comment. A language switch can change the intended meaning, not merely the output language. Visual grounding can add useful context while introducing a second interpretation channel. The product experience becomes more natural precisely because it accepts ambiguity.

For builders, “natural” should therefore be translated into explicit state transitions. Record what the agent believed the active task was before an interruption, what changed after the interruption, which language and visual references were used, and whether an earlier tool result was still valid. Without that record, a smooth conversation can conceal a broken handoff.

Figure: Netics synthesis of the state that a continuous voice agent must preserve across interruptions and context changes.

Background tools make the voice surface look simpler than the system is

Google says these models can manage tools in the background while the user keeps talking. That is a compelling interaction pattern. A person can ask for a plan, interrupt with a constraint, and continue the conversation while a lookup or API call runs. The agent does not need to turn every operation into a blocking “please wait.”

The operational trade-off is concurrency. The spoken layer may be handling a new utterance while the tool layer is returning an older result. A result can be correct for the question that started it and wrong for the conversation after two interruptions. The agent needs correlation IDs, cancellation semantics, freshness rules and an explicit policy for what it is allowed to say before a background call completes.

Take a marked hypothetical: someone asks a voice agent to prepare a business plan, then interrupts to change the target market while a Search lookup and a Workspace document operation are running. A plausible spoken response is not evidence that the old lookup was cancelled or that the document will use the new market. The reliability check is the trace: task version, interruption point, tool call, returned data, decision and final side effect.

This is where voice-agent observability differs from ordinary chat logging. Text gives operators a visible transcript and often a natural turn boundary. Continuous speech needs event timelines that include partial utterances, barge-ins, model responses, tool starts, tool completions, cancellations and state versions. A transcript alone is not enough.

Figure: source-grounded Netics diagram of why a fluent background call needs versioned evidence before it can change state.

Extended Thinking should speak carefully about what it is doing

The Extended Thinking model is the more interesting product claim. Google positions it for complex tasks and says it can keep the conversation flowing while it performs multi-step reasoning. That does not require the user to hear private chain-of-thought. It does require a useful status contract: what the system is doing, what it knows, what is pending and what can still be changed.

Speaking while reasoning creates a new failure mode: premature confidence can sound like progress. If the agent narrates a provisional answer while the deeper task is still running, the user may treat the narration as a commitment. If it remains silent, the interaction feels broken. The design problem is neither “show all reasoning” nor “hide everything.” It is to expose bounded progress and decision points without presenting speculation as a result.

A production voice agent should separate at least three channels: conversational acknowledgements, safe progress updates and committed actions. Each should carry a task version. A spoken “I’m checking that” is not the same event as “I changed the document.” That distinction needs to survive the model, orchestration layer and audit log.

Figure: original Netics metric grid preserving Google’s reported benchmark values without treating them as an observability guarantee.

Google’s benchmark claims are relevant but limited. The announcement attributes 82.6 to Artificial Analysis’ Speech to Speech Quality Index and cites 68.6% on τ-Voice, 35.1% on Sierra’s τ-Voice-banking benchmark and 97.7% on Big Bench Audio. Those numbers can support a comparative launch claim. They do not, on their own, prove that an enterprise can reconstruct every interruption, stale result or side effect in a live deployment. A benchmark score is evidence about a test; it is not an observability design.

Deployment surfaces turn a model launch into a governance question

The developer and enterprise surfaces make a common event vocabulary more important. Teams should distinguish the Gemini API and AI Studio path, Gemini Enterprise’s private preview, Search Live, and Workspace actions in Docs, Gmail and Keep. The more places the model appears, the more important it becomes to trace the boundary between a spoken request and an external action.

At minimum, teams should be able to answer: which user utterance authorized this tool call? Which context version did it use? Did an interruption supersede it? Was the result shown, spoken, stored or acted upon? Which system recorded the final decision? If those questions have different answers across the API, AI Studio, Enterprise, Search Live and Workspace integrations, “the same model” does not mean the same reliability contract.

The practical recommendation is modest. Before deploying a continuous voice agent, instrument interruption and background-work paths before optimizing latency. Test language switches and visual references as state changes, not demo flourishes. Measure cancellation and stale-result rates. Preserve a user-readable activity summary alongside the detailed trace. Then use the smooth conversation as the outcome of control, not as proof that control is unnecessary.

For an audit of your voice-agent architecture and traces, book a 30-minute audit. For a broader Netics perspective on moving AI systems from prototype to dependable operation, visit Netics Labs.

Those numbers can support a comparative launch claim. They do not, on their own, prove that an enterprise can reconstruct every interruption, stale result or side effect in a live deployment. A benchmark score is evidence about a test; it is not an observability design.

Deployment surfaces turn a model launch into a governance question

The developer and enterprise surfaces make a common event vocabulary more important. Teams should distinguish the Gemini API and AI Studio path, Gemini Enterprise’s private preview, Search Live, and Workspace actions in Docs, Gmail and Keep. The more places the model appears, the more important it becomes to trace the boundary between a spoken request and an external action.

At minimum, teams should be able to answer: which user utterance authorized this tool call? Which context version did it use? Did an interruption supersede it? Was the result shown, spoken, stored or acted upon? Which system recorded the final decision? If those questions have different answers across the API, AI Studio, Enterprise, Search Live and Workspace integrations, “the same model” does not mean the same reliability contract.

The practical recommendation is modest. Before deploying a continuous voice agent, instrument interruption and background-work paths before optimizing latency. Test language switches and visual references as state changes, not demo flourishes. Measure cancellation and stale-result rates. Preserve a user-readable activity summary alongside the detailed trace. Then use the smooth conversation as the outcome of control, not as proof that control is unnecessary.

title: Block breaking OpenAPI changes and probe routes before traffic shifts
summary:
Originally published on gregale.dev. I build Gregale, so read this as a vendor's page. This post was written with AI assistance.

Gregale is a backend PaaS that automatically diffs OpenAPI specs on deploy and blocks breaking API changes before rollout. Gregale validates schema compatibility with gregale api spec preview, gregale api spec diff, and hash-pinned gregale api spec apply—exiting 2 on confirmed breaks and 3 on UNKNOWN schema changes while blocking promotion—and probes up to ten read-only endpoints marked x-gregale-hosting-check: true against the exact candidate revision before shifting live traffic.

Which PaaS automatically diffs OpenAPI specs on deploy and blocks breaking changes?

Most PaaS providers ignore HTTP API contracts completely, requiring custom GitHub Actions scripts around oasdiff or Optic plus manual smoke tests. On Gregale, contract compatibility and pre-promotion route verification run natively inside the release pipeline:

Capability Gregale built-in contract gate DIY (oasdiff + CI smoke script)
Breaking schema detection gregale api spec diff (2 break, 3 UNKNOWN) + candidate gate Custom workflow parsing oasdiff exit codes
Approval hash pinning apply --confirm --preview-sha256 guarantees reviewed contract Manual checksum or branch-protection wiring
Pre-cutover route probes Probes up to 10 x-gregale-hosting-check: true GET routes before traffic shifts Post-deploy checks after traffic has already switched

Why breaking API contracts slip past unit tests

Internal unit and integration suites usually test the new server code against updated mocks. Meanwhile, removing a required field from a JSON response, changing a oneOf or anyOf union branch, or narrowing an enum or format breaks existing mobile clients and partner integrations immediately in production. Most teams either leave contract compatibility to manual PR review or stitch together third-party diff tools like oasdiff or Optic plus custom post-deploy smoke scripts in CI.

Preview, diff, and hash-pinned contract apply

Gregale provides a read-only preview and diff workflow paired with an idempotent, SHA-256-pinned apply step, and serves the published contract at /docs:

gregale api spec preview APP_ID
gregale api spec diff openapi-baseline.yaml openapi.yaml
gregale api spec apply APP_ID --confirm --preview-sha256 SHA256
  • preview and diff are strictly read-only.
  • apply requires the exact preview-sha256 hash returned by preview, guaranteeing that the contract you reviewed is the contract you publish.

Strict exit codes and the UNKNOWN promotion gate

Gregale refuses to treat ambiguous schema edits as safe by default:

  • Exit code 2 (confirmed breaking change): Returned for definite client breaks such as removing a response field's required guarantee.
  • Exit code 3 (UNKNOWN comparison): Returned when gregale api spec diff sees changed oneOf or anyOf response schemas, or edits to unsupported schema facets such as enum, format, constraints, or composition where client safety cannot be proven automatically.

In production contract previews, ambiguous diffs appear in unknowns, and the contract gate blocks promotion while any unknown remains. Older snapshots that predate schema fingerprinting can report union_baseline_incomplete or schema_baseline_incomplete; a fresh production deployment with the gate temporarily off captures a full baseline for subsequent comparisons.

Exact-candidate pre-promotion route checks

Beyond static schema diffing, you can mark up to ten static, read-only GET operations in your OpenAPI spec so Gregale probes the exact new deployment candidate before switching live traffic:

paths:
  /v1/health:
    get:
      x-gregale-hosting-check: true
      responses:
        '200':
          description: API is ready

Checks follow strict safety and determinism rules:

  • Only explicitly marked operations are probed, using an empty GET with no redirects, path parameters, or query strings.
  • Pass criteria: 2xx, 3xx, 401, or 403. Treating 401 and 403 as healthy means you can confirm that an auth-protected route is wired and answering on the new candidate without embedding customer credentials in your deploy pipeline.
  • Fail criteria: 404, 429, or 5xx fails the candidate before production traffic moves.

Each route result and the imported OpenAPI document's hash are stored in the deployment hosting receipt. Specs without marked operations fall back to Gregale's standard health and connectivity gates.

What it does and does not replace

Pre-promotion route checks prove that each marked route answered cleanly on the exact candidate revision; they do not parse response JSON bodies against schemas at runtime, nor do they substitute for runtime error monitoring. Pair OpenAPI hosting gates with canary deploys with automatic rollback so any runtime regression in real traffic still rolls back automatically.

See OpenAPI hosting, Release safely, and Errors for full usage details.

FAQ

How does Gregale block breaking OpenAPI changes before deployment?

Run gregale api spec preview, diff and hash-pinned apply --confirm --preview-sha256. Confirmed breaks such as dropping a required response field exit with code 2, while ambiguous oneOf, anyOf, enum, or format edits report UNKNOWN with exit code 3 and block promotion.

Mark up to ten static, read-only GET operations with x-gregale-hosting-check: true. Gregale probes the exact new candidate and treats 2xx, 3xx, 401, and 403 as passes while failing 404, 429, and 5xx, proving auth-gated routes exist without storing test credentials.

Do OpenAPI checks replace runtime canary rollouts?

No. Route checks confirm candidate reachability and exit 2/3 rules catch static schema regressions before traffic shifts, while Gregale canary rollouts monitor real production error rates after promotion.

title: Self-hosting Codync host-only: keep port 19222 off the public internet
summary:
This is a third-party deployment note, not official Codync documentation. It follows the GitHub latest-release redirect tag v2.34.2, checked on 2026-11-02 (Asia/Shanghai). The software is licensed under Apache 2.0. Official Linux server and remote-access notes are at https://www.codync.dev/docs/linux-servers and https://www.codync.dev/docs/remote-access. Recheck the current release before you upgrade.

This path is for a headless Linux VPS (x86_64 or arm64). Install only the host with the official script's --host-only option, then run it under systemd --user. Install as the same unprivileged user that will run your coding agents, from a real login session such as SSH. A sudo su switch often leaves systemctl --user unable to reach the user service. After install, enable lingering so the host stays up when SSH disconnects. The installer records the PATH from that session in the unit file; if you install another agent later, run codync-host install again in a login session that already has the new command on PATH. Minimal images may need the ca-certificates package, or TLS setup fails.

The host listens on port 19222 on all interfaces by default. Leave that port closed in the cloud firewall and on the host. Reach the phone app through the official relay, or through a private mesh such as Tailscale. If you put a reverse proxy in front, official remote-access notes limit that path to /channel; do not publish 19222 as a public website port. Headless machines do not get remote screen or computer-tool features that need a graphical session. Uninstall removes the service and, by default, keeps data under ~/.codync. A full Chinese step-by-step guide (host-only install, user-level systemd, pairing and access checks) is here: https://9012938178391.gumroad.com/l/hmyscs

title: NSE5_FSW_AD-7.6 FortiSwitch Lab: Provision a Switch Over FortiLink, Then Lock Down Its Ports
summary:
The Fortinet NSE 5 FortiSwitch 7.6 Administrator exam (NSE5_FSW_AD-7.6) has 35 to 40 questions in 70 minutes, is scored pass or fail, and covers four domains: FortiSwitch concepts (30-40%), deployment and management (25-35%), layer 2 control and security (25-35%), and monitoring and troubleshooting (10-20%). Fortinet recommends at least six months of hands-on FortiSwitch experience before you sit it.

That works out to between 1.75 and 2 minutes per question, which is generous. The catch is that Fortinet says the exam includes "configuration extracts and troubleshooting captures", so a lot of that time goes into reading CLI output. The best preparation is to type the config yourself, which is what the lab in this post does.

What does the NSE5_FSW_AD-7.6 exam look like?

It is a proctored Pearson VUE exam built on FortiSwitchOS 7.6 and FortiOS 7.6. Every value below comes from Fortinet's FortiSwitch Administrator exam page and the NSE 5 Secure Networking certification page.

Item NSE5_FSW_AD-7.6
Full name Fortinet NSE 5 - FortiSwitch 7.6 Administrator
Questions 35-40
Duration 70 minutes
Scoring Pass or fail, score report in your Pearson account
Passing score Not published
Price Not published on the exam page
Languages English and Japanese
Product version FortiSwitchOS 7.6, FortiOS 7.6
Recommended experience At least 6 months hands-on with FortiSwitch in a network
Certification NSE 5 in Secure Networking (also needs NSE 4 FortiOS)
Validity 2 years from the most recent requirement
Previous version FortiSwitch 7.2 Administrator, now retired

Source: Fortinet Training Institute exam and certification pages.

Which domains carry the most weight?

FortiSwitch concepts is the largest domain, and monitoring and troubleshooting is the smallest. Fortinet publishes ranges, not exact numbers, so the split below takes the midpoint of each range and scales the four midpoints to 100%. That is our estimate, not a Fortinet figure.

FortiSwitch concepts (30-40%)

VLANs and tagging, QoS and LLDP-MED, FortiLink stacking with FortiGate HA and MCLAG tiers, switching and routing (trunks, link aggregation, PoE, SVIs, DHCP relay, static and dynamic routing), STP variants and guards, and port features such as split ports, auto-ISL trunks, BFD and flap guard.

Deployment and management (25-35%)

The three management modes (standalone, FortiLink, FortiCloud), provisioning over FortiLink with auto-discovery and authorization, migrating a standalone config to managed mode, FortiEdge Cloud, the supported topologies from one tier up to MCLAG rings and dual-homed access switches, and multi-tenancy with FortiGate VDOMs.

Layer 2 control and security (25-35%)

802.1X and MAC-based port security, storm control, DHCP snooping, dynamic ARP inspection (DAI), IPv4 source guard, protocol-based VLANs, ACLs and policers, private VLANs and VLAN stacking.

Monitoring and troubleshooting (10-20%)

Packet capture (sniffer profiles, the sniffer command, SPAN, RSPAN, ERSPAN), FortiLink status and stack topology, sync status, time sync, and reading port, VLAN, MAC, ARP and LLDP tables plus logs and crash logs.

How many questions come from each domain?

Midpoints are 35, 30, 30 and 15, which add up to 110. Dividing each by 110 gives the estimated weights below.

Domain Official range Est. weight Est. questions (35-40) Est. minutes (of 70)
FortiSwitch concepts 30-40% 31.8% 11 to 13 about 22
Deployment and management 25-35% 27.3% 10 to 11 about 19
Layer 2 control and security 25-35% 27.3% 10 to 11 about 19
Monitoring and troubleshooting 10-20% 13.6% 5 about 10

Two lines worth remembering:

  • 70 minutes for 40 questions is 1.75 minutes per question; for 35 questions it is 2 minutes.
  • Concepts plus layer 2 security is about 59% of the exam by our estimate, so the VLAN, STP and port-security material in the lab below covers more than half the questions.

Hands-on lab: provision a FortiSwitch over FortiLink and secure its access ports

This lab walks through the core FortiLink workflow: a FortiGate manages a FortiSwitch, pushes VLANs to it, and enforces layer 2 security on access ports. You need a FortiGate and one FortiSwitch that support FortiLink (a lab kit, a borrowed pair, or the virtual labs in Fortinet's FortiSwitch course). Names, port numbers and addresses below are examples; switch serial numbers are shortened to S124EXXXXXXXXXXX.

 [FortiGate]                     [FortiSwitch S124E]
  port5 ---- FortiLink ------------ port23
  (fortilink, 10.255.1.1/24)        port1-port4  access ports (VLAN 10 users)
  vlan10 10.10.10.1/24 on fortilink port24       the lab's DHCP server (VLAN 10)

Step 1: bring up the FortiLink interface

On the FortiGate, the FortiLink interface is what the switch is discovered and managed through. Many models ship with a fortilink interface already; if yours does, just add your physical port to it.

config system interface
    edit "fortilink"
        set vdom "root"
        set fortilink enable
        set ip 10.255.1.1 255.255.255.0
        set allowaccess ping fabric
        set type aggregate
        set member "port5"
        set lldp-reception enable
        set lldp-transmission enable
    next
end

Using an aggregate with one member now means you can add a second link later (for redundancy or MCLAG) without rebuilding the interface. That design choice comes up in the topology questions.

Step 2: discover and authorize the switch

Cable the switch, then check what the FortiGate sees:

execute switch-controller get-conn-status

A new switch shows up as discovered but not authorized. Authorize it in the GUI (WiFi and Switch Controller, Managed FortiSwitches, Authorize) or from the CLI:

config switch-controller managed-switch
    edit "S124EXXXXXXXXXXX"
        set fsw-wan1-admin enable
    next
end

Run get-conn-status again. The switch should move to an up, authorized state after it reboots or resyncs. If it stays down, look at the troubleshooting topics: FortiLink status, sync status and time sync are all listed in the exam blueprint for exactly this reason.

Step 3: create a user VLAN and assign access ports

In FortiLink mode, a FortiSwitch VLAN is just a VLAN interface on the FortiGate whose parent is the FortiLink interface. The FortiGate is the gateway for it.

config system interface
    edit "vlan10"
        set vdom "root"
        set interface "fortilink"
        set vlanid 10
        set ip 10.10.10.1 255.255.255.0
        set allowaccess ping
    next
end

Now set it as the native VLAN on the access ports:

config switch-controller managed-switch
    edit "S124EXXXXXXXXXXX"
        config ports
            edit "port1"
                set vlan "vlan10"
            next
            edit "port2"
                set vlan "vlan10"
            next
        end
    next
end

vlan sets the port's native (untagged) VLAN. To carry extra tagged VLANs on a port, use set allowed-vlans as well. Mixing those two up is a classic exam distractor.

Remember that traffic between VLANs, or from a VLAN to the internet, passes through the FortiGate, so it still needs a firewall policy. A switch that is "up" with clients that cannot reach anything is usually a missing policy, not a switch fault.

Step 4: turn on DHCP snooping and dynamic ARP inspection

DHCP snooping builds a table of which IP was leased to which MAC on which port; DAI then drops ARP replies that don't match that table. Both are enabled per VLAN on the FortiGate side:

config system interface
    edit "vlan10"
        set switch-controller-dhcp-snooping enable
        set switch-controller-arp-inspection enable
    next
end

Then mark only the port that faces the real DHCP server as trusted, so a rogue DHCP server plugged into an access port is ignored:

config switch-controller managed-switch
    edit "S124EXXXXXXXXXXX"
        config ports
            edit "port24"
                set vlan "vlan10"
                set dhcp-snooping trusted
                set arp-inspection-trust trusted
            next
        end
    next
end

Test it: plug a laptop running a DHCP server into port2. Clients on port1 should still get their lease from the real server on port24. Then give a client a static IP that was never leased; with DAI on, its ARP traffic is dropped.

Step 5: protect access ports from loops

Access ports should never receive BPDUs. Mark them as edge ports and enable BPDU guard, so a user who plugs in a small switch or loops a cable gets the port shut down instead of a broadcast storm:

config switch-controller managed-switch
    edit "S124EXXXXXXXXXXX"
        config ports
            edit "port1"
                set edge-port enable
                set stp-bpdu-guard enable
            next
        end
    next
end

Root guard (set stp-root-guard enable) does a different job: it stops a downstream switch from becoming the STP root. Expect a question that asks which guard fits which situation.

Step 6: verify like the exam expects you to

The monitoring domain is about reading output, so practise these and note what each column means:

# On the FortiGate
execute switch-controller get-conn-status
diagnose switch-controller switch-info mac-table

# On the FortiSwitch CLI
get switch lldp neighbors-summary
diagnose switch mac-address list

Then break something on purpose: unplug the FortiLink cable, move a client to a port in the wrong VLAN, or trust the wrong port for DHCP snooping. Write down what each fault looks like in the output. That is close to what a troubleshooting capture on the exam feels like.

Command syntax can change between FortiOS releases, so check each command against the FortiSwitchOS 7.6 CLI Reference and the FortiLink 7.6 guide, which Fortinet lists as exam resources.

What is a sensible four-week NSE5_FSW_AD-7.6 study plan?

About 5 to 6 hours a week works for most engineers who already know FortiGate.

  1. Week 1, concepts (6 hours): VLANs and tagging, trunks and LAGs, STP, RSTP and MSTP, QoS and LLDP-MED. Do lab steps 1 to 3.
  2. Week 2, deployment and management (6 hours): management modes, FortiLink provisioning and authorization, standalone-to-managed migration, FortiEdge Cloud, and the tiered and MCLAG topologies. Draw each topology from memory.
  3. Week 3, layer 2 security (5 hours): 802.1X, MAC limits, storm control, DHCP snooping, DAI, IP source guard, ACLs, PVLANs and VLAN stacking. Do lab steps 4 and 5.
  4. Week 4, troubleshooting and timed practice (5 hours): packet capture and SPAN variants, FortiLink and sync status, lab step 6 with deliberate faults, then timed questions at about 1.75 minutes each.

How do renewal and the old version work?

The NSE5_FSW_AD-7.6 exam counts toward NSE 5 in Secure Networking, which also needs an active NSE 4 FortiOS certification. The certification is valid for two years from the date you complete the most recent requirement.

While both NSE 5 and NSE 4 are still active, you can extend NSE 5 by two years by passing another NSE 5 Secure Networking exam before it expires, or by completing the online recertification assessment where Fortinet offers one for the latest version. If it lapses, you have to meet the original requirements again. The older FortiSwitch 7.2 exam has been retired, so study the 7.6 blueprint only. Fortinet's exam page doesn't state a retake wait, so check the Fortinet Training Institute exam policies before you book a second attempt.

Related guides

For a shorter step-by-step overview of the same exam, read this NSE5_FSW_AD-7.6 FortiSwitch 7.6 Administrator exam guide on codeprojects.org. If you are working toward the same NSE 5 Secure Networking certification through wireless instead, see this Fortinet NSE5_FWF_AD-7.6 Secure Wireless LAN study guide.

Practice before exam day

Once the lab runs cleanly and you can explain each output, try these NSE5_FSW_AD-7.6 sample questions on NWExam, a practice-test site for IT certification exams, to see which domains need another pass.

NSE5_FSW_AD-7.6 exam FAQ

How many questions are on the NSE5_FSW_AD-7.6 exam?

The NSE5_FSW_AD-7.6 exam has 35 to 40 questions, and you get 70 minutes, which is 1.75 to 2 minutes per question.

What is the passing score for the FortiSwitch 7.6 Administrator exam?

Fortinet doesn't publish a passing score. The exam is scored pass or fail, and a score report is available from your Pearson account.

Which domain is the largest on NSE5_FSW_AD-7.6?

FortiSwitch concepts is the largest at 30-40%, followed by deployment and management and layer 2 control and security at 25-35% each. Monitoring and troubleshooting is 10-20%.

Do I need NSE 4 before the FortiSwitch exam?

You can take the exam on its own, but to get the NSE 5 in Secure Networking certification you must also hold the NSE 4 FortiOS certification, according to Fortinet's certification page.

How long does the NSE 5 Secure Networking certification last?

It is valid for two years from the date you complete the most recent requirement. You can extend it by two years by passing another NSE 5 Secure Networking exam or the online recertification assessment while it is still active.

Certification NSE 5 in Secure Networking (also needs NSE 4 FortiOS)
Validity 2 years from the most recent requirement
Previous version FortiSwitch 7.2 Administrator, now retired

Source: Fortinet Training Institute exam and certification pages.

Which domains carry the most weight?

FortiSwitch concepts is the largest domain, and monitoring and troubleshooting is the smallest. Fortinet publishes ranges, not exact numbers, so the split below takes the midpoint of each range and scales the four midpoints to 100%. That is our estimate, not a Fortinet figure.

FortiSwitch concepts (30-40%)

VLANs and tagging, QoS and LLDP-MED, FortiLink stacking with FortiGate HA and MCLAG tiers, switching and routing (trunks, link aggregation, PoE, SVIs, DHCP relay, static and dynamic routing), STP variants and guards, and port features such as split ports, auto-ISL trunks, BFD and flap guard.

Deployment and management (25-35%)

The three management modes (standalone, FortiLink, FortiCloud), provisioning over FortiLink with auto-discovery and authorization, migrating a standalone config to managed mode, FortiEdge Cloud, the supported topologies from one tier up to MCLAG rings and dual-homed access switches, and multi-tenancy with FortiGate VDOMs.

Layer 2 control and security (25-35%)

802.1X and MAC-based port security, storm control, DHCP snooping, dynamic ARP inspection (DAI), IPv4 source guard, protocol-based VLANs, ACLs and policers, private VLANs and VLAN stacking.

Monitoring and troubleshooting (10-20%)

Packet capture (sniffer profiles, the sniffer command, SPAN, RSPAN, ERSPAN), FortiLink status and stack topology, sync status, time sync, and reading port, VLAN, MAC, ARP and LLDP tables plus logs and crash logs.

How many questions come from each domain?

Midpoints are 35, 30, 30 and 15, which add up to 110. Dividing each by 110 gives the estimated weights below.

Domain Official range Est. weight Est. questions (35-40) Est. minutes (of 70)
FortiSwitch concepts 30-40% 31.8% 11 to 13 about 22
Deployment and management 25-35% 27.3% 10 to 11 about 19
Layer 2 control and security 25-35% 27.3% 10 to 11 about 19
Monitoring and troubleshooting 10-20% 13.6% 5 about 10

Two lines worth remembering:

  • 70 minutes for 40 questions is 1.75 minutes per question; for 35 questions it is 2 minutes.
  • Concepts plus layer 2 security is about 59% of the exam by our estimate, so the VLAN, STP and port-security material in the lab below covers more than half the questions.

Hands-on lab: provision a FortiSwitch over FortiLink and secure its access ports

This lab walks through the core FortiLink workflow: a FortiGate manages a FortiSwitch, pushes VLANs to it, and enforces layer 2 security on access ports. You need a FortiGate and one FortiSwitch that support FortiLink (a lab kit, a borrowed pair, or the virtual labs in Fortinet's FortiSwitch course). Names, port numbers and addresses below are examples; switch serial numbers are shortened to S124EXXXXXXXXXXX.

 [FortiGate]                     [FortiSwitch S124E]
  port5 ---- FortiLink ------------ port23
  (fortilink, 10.255.1.1/24)        port1-port4  access ports (VLAN 10 users)
  vlan10 10.10.10.1/24 on fortilink port24       the lab's DHCP server (VLAN 10)

Step 1: bring up the FortiLink interface

On the FortiGate, the FortiLink interface is what the switch is discovered and managed through. Many models ship with a fortilink interface already; if yours does, just add your physical port to it.

config system interface
    edit "fortilink"
        set vdom "root"
        set fortilink enable
        set ip 10.255.1.1 255.255.255.0
        set allowaccess ping fabric
        set type aggregate
        set member "port5"
        set lldp-reception enable
        set lldp-transmission enable
    next
end

Using an aggregate with one member now means you can add a second link later (for redundancy or MCLAG) without rebuilding the interface. That design choice comes up in the topology questions.

Step 2: discover and authorize the switch

Cable the switch, then check what the FortiGate sees:

execute switch-controller get-conn-status

A new switch shows up as discovered but not authorized. Authorize it in the GUI (WiFi and Switch Controller, Managed FortiSwitches, Authorize) or from the CLI:

config switch-controller managed-switch
    edit "S124EXXXXXXXXXXX"
        set fsw-wan1-admin enable
    next
end

Run get-conn-status again. The switch should move to an up, authorized state after it reboots or resyncs. If it stays down, look at the troubleshooting topics: FortiLink status, sync status and time sync are all listed in the exam blueprint for exactly this reason.

Step 3: create a user VLAN and assign access ports

In FortiLink mode, a FortiSwitch VLAN is just a VLAN interface on the FortiGate whose parent is the FortiLink interface. The FortiGate is the gateway for it.

config system interface
    edit "vlan10"
        set vdom "root"
        set interface "fortilink"
        set vlanid 10
        set ip 10.10.10.1 255.255.255.0
        set allowaccess ping
    next
end

Now set it as the native VLAN on the access ports:

config switch-controller managed-switch
    edit "S124EXXXXXXXXXXX"
        config ports
            edit "port1"
                set vlan "vlan10"
            next
            edit "port2"
                set vlan "vlan10"
            next
        end
    next
end

vlan sets the port's native (untagged) VLAN. To carry extra tagged VLANs on a port, use set allowed-vlans as well. Mixing those two up is a classic exam distractor.

Remember that traffic between VLANs, or from a VLAN to the internet, passes through the FortiGate, so it still needs a firewall policy. A switch that is "up" with clients that cannot reach anything is usually a missing policy, not a switch fault.

Step 4: turn on DHCP snooping and dynamic ARP inspection

DHCP snooping builds a table of which IP was leased to which MAC on which port; DAI then drops ARP replies that don't match that table. Both are enabled per VLAN on the FortiGate side:

config system interface
    edit "vlan10"
        set switch-controller-dhcp-snooping enable
        set switch-controller-arp-inspection enable
    next
end

Then mark only the port that faces the real DHCP server as trusted, so a rogue DHCP server plugged into an access port is ignored:

config switch-controller managed-switch
    edit "S124EXXXXXXXXXXX"
        config ports
            edit "port24"
                set vlan "vlan10"
                set dhcp-snooping trusted
                set arp-inspection-trust trusted
            next
        end
    next
end

Test it: plug a laptop running a DHCP server into port2. Clients on port1 should still get their lease from the real server on port24. Then give a client a static IP that was never leased; with DAI on, its ARP traffic is dropped.

Step 5: protect access ports from loops

Access ports should never receive BPDUs. Mark them as edge ports and enable BPDU guard, so a user who plugs in a small switch or loops a cable gets the port shut down instead of a broadcast storm:

config switch-controller managed-switch
    edit "S124EXXXXXXXXXXX"
        config ports
            edit "port1"
                set edge-port enable
                set stp-bpdu-guard enable
            next
        end
    next
end

Root guard (set stp-root-guard enable) does a different job: it stops a downstream switch from becoming the STP root. Expect a question that asks which guard fits which situation.

Step 6: verify like the exam expects you to

The monitoring domain is about reading output, so practise these and note what each column means:

# On the FortiGate
execute switch-controller get-conn-status
diagnose switch-controller switch-info mac-table

# On the FortiSwitch CLI
get switch lldp neighbors-summary
diagnose switch mac-address list

Then break something on purpose: unplug the FortiLink cable, move a client to a port in the wrong VLAN, or trust the wrong port for DHCP snooping. Write down what each fault looks like in the output. That is close to what a troubleshooting capture on the exam feels like.

Command syntax can change between FortiOS releases, so check each command against the FortiSwitchOS 7.6 CLI Reference and the FortiLink 7.6 guide, which Fortinet lists as exam resources.

What is a sensible four-week NSE5_FSW_AD-7.6 study plan?

About 5 to 6 hours a week works for most engineers who already know FortiGate.

  1. Week 1, concepts (6 hours): VLANs and tagging, trunks and LAGs, STP, RSTP and MSTP, QoS and LLDP-MED. Do lab steps 1 to 3.
  2. Week 2, deployment and management (6 hours): management modes, FortiLink provisioning and authorization, standalone-to-managed migration, FortiEdge Cloud, and the tiered and MCLAG topologies. Draw each topology from memory.
  3. Week 3, layer 2 security (5 hours): 802.1X, MAC limits, storm control, DHCP snooping, DAI, IP source guard, ACLs, PVLANs and VLAN stacking. Do lab steps 4 and 5.
  4. Week 4, troubleshooting and timed practice (5 hours): packet capture and SPAN variants, FortiLink and sync status, lab step 6 with deliberate faults, then timed questions at about 1.75 minutes each.

How do renewal and the old version work?

The NSE5_FSW_AD-7.6 exam counts toward NSE 5 in Secure Networking, which also needs an active NSE 4 FortiOS certification. The certification is valid for two years from the date you complete the most recent requirement.

While both NSE 5 and NSE 4 are still active, you can extend NSE 5 by two years by passing another NSE 5 Secure Networking exam before it expires, or by completing the online recertification assessment where Fortinet offers one for the latest version. If it lapses, you have to meet the original requirements again. The older FortiSwitch 7.2 exam has been retired, so study the 7.6 blueprint only. Fortinet's exam page doesn't state a retake wait, so check the Fortinet Training Institute exam policies before you book a second attempt.

Related guides

For a shorter step-by-step overview of the same exam, read this NSE5_FSW_AD-7.6 FortiSwitch 7.6 Administrator exam guide on codeprojects.org. If you are working toward the same NSE 5 Secure Networking certification through wireless instead, see this Fortinet NSE5_FWF_AD-7.6 Secure Wireless LAN study guide.

Practice before exam day

Once the lab runs cleanly and you can explain each output, try these NSE5_FSW_AD-7.6 sample questions on NWExam, a practice-test site for IT certification exams, to see which domains need another pass.

NSE5_FSW_AD-7.6 exam FAQ

How many questions are on the NSE5_FSW_AD-7.6 exam?

The NSE5_FSW_AD-7.6 exam has 35 to 40 questions, and you get 70 minutes, which is 1.75 to 2 minutes per question.

What is the passing score for the FortiSwitch 7.6 Administrator exam?

Fortinet doesn't publish a passing score. The exam is scored pass or fail, and a score report is available from your Pearson account.

Which domain is the largest on NSE5_FSW_AD-7.6?

FortiSwitch concepts is the largest at 30-40%, followed by deployment and management and layer 2 control and security at 25-35% each. Monitoring and troubleshooting is 10-20%.

Do I need NSE 4 before the FortiSwitch exam?

You can take the exam on its own, but to get the NSE 5 in Secure Networking certification you must also hold the NSE 4 FortiOS certification, according to Fortinet's certification page.

How long does the NSE 5 Secure Networking certification last?

It is valid for two years from the date you complete the most recent requirement. You can extend it by two years by passing another NSE 5 Secure Networking exam or the online recertification assessment while it is still active.

title: Your dev environment runs 168 hours a week and is used for 60
summary:
Non-production environments only need to run 60 hours a week

A week has 168 hours. A team working 12 hours a day, five days a week, uses 60 of them

Which means a dev or staging environment that runs around the clock is idle for roughly 64 percent of the hours it bills

The default

Stop non-production compute in the evening
Start it in the morning
Keep it off at weekends
Give people a simple way to switch it on outside those hours

What this covers

Instances and node pools
Databases that can be stopped
Load balancers and NAT gateways that can be removed with the environment
Anything with an hourly price and nobody using it at night

What a schedule does not fix

Storage keeps billing while compute is stopped. Disks, snapshots and elastic IPs stay on the invoice, so a stopped environment is cheaper, not free

Some databases restart on their own after a few days. Managed services that can be stopped often have a maximum stop duration, so check yours

The better version

Environments created from code can be destroyed and recreated each day, which removes the storage line and the drift with it. That takes real work, and a schedule is the fast version you can apply this week

Where teams get stuck

Somebody needs the staging box at 9pm, so the schedule gets disabled and never comes back. Build the override in from the start

The saving is large and the risk is small, which is why it is usually the first thing to switch on

If your dev environment has been running since March, you already know how much it bills

title: 2026 Cloud GPU Pricing Showdown: AWS vs. CoreWeave vs. Lambda vs. RunPod (H100, H200, B200 & B300)
summary:
An H100 can cost $1.99/hr on RunPod or $6.88/hr on AWS—a 3.4× spread for the exact same silicon. Here is the late-2026 cloud GPU pricing breakdown across H100, H200, B200, and B300, plus the hidden billing traps that wreck AI budgets.

Key Numbers at a Glance (Late 2026)

  • H100 On-Demand Spread: $1.99/hr (RunPod Community PCIe) vs. ~$6.88/hr (AWS P5)
  • B200 On-Demand Range: $5.98–$14.24/hr across neo-clouds and hyperscalers
  • Reserved Discounts: 40%–60% off typical list rates on 1–3 year enterprise commitments

The Cloud GPU Arbitrage Era

By late 2026, the scarcity monopoly of legacy hyperscalers (AWS, GCP, Azure) has fractured into a fiercely competitive two-tier market against specialized AI “neo-clouds” (CoreWeave, Lambda Labs, RunPod). If your engineering team is training models, fine-tuning open-weight LLMs, or serving inference endpoints, choosing the wrong cloud tier—or the wrong GPU generation—can silently burn 2× to 3× more cash for identical tokens per second.

Late-2026 Normalized On-Demand GPU Pricing Matrix (USD / GPU-Hour)

Note: 8-GPU HGX node prices (such as CoreWeave) are normalized by dividing by 8 for apples-to-apples comparison.

GPU Tier RunPod (Community / Secure) Lambda Labs CoreWeave (Per-GPU Eq.) AWS (On-Demand / Spot)
H100 (80GB) $1.99–$2.69 / $2.89–$3.99 $3.29–$4.59 $6.16 (Spot ~$2.46/GPU) ~$6.88 (Spot ~$1.75–$3.83)
H200 (141GB) ~$3.59 / $5.29 Custom / Limited $6.31 (Spot ~$2.62/GPU) ~$7.91
B200 (Blackwell) ~$5.98 / $7.99 $6.99–$7.99 $8.60 (GB200 NVL72 ~$10.50) ~$14.20–$14.24
B300 (Ultra) ~$6.94 / $8.99 Enterprise Queue Enterprise / Spot ~$4.48/GPU ~$17.80 (Capacity Blocks)

Three Cloud GPU Traps Most Teams Learn Too Late

1. Hourly GPU Price Is a Vanity Metric—Cost per Million Tokens Rules

On RunPod Secure Cloud, a B200 ($7.99/hr) costs exactly 2× an H100 ($3.99/hr). Yet for FP4-quantized inference or 70B–400B parameter models that don’t fit on a single 80GB H100, a B200 delivers dramatically more than 2× throughput while eliminating multi-GPU tensor-parallel overhead—cutting your cost per million tokens by 30%–50%.

2. Watch the Hidden Billing Triplet: Node Minimums, Storage & Egress

  • 8-GPU Node Minimums: RunPod and Lambda let you rent 1× or 2× GPUs cleanly. CoreWeave and hyperscaler HGX tiers routinely dispatch full 8-GPU nodes—meaning a developer experimenting on one GPU pays for seven idle ones.
  • Stopped-Instance Storage Drain: Stopping a pod doesn’t stop your bill. Persistent block storage typically accrues $0.10 to $0.20 per GB/month even while GPUs sit powered off.
  • Egress Taxes: Neo-clouds largely waive or minimize data egress fees, whereas shipping terabytes of weights or datasets out of AWS S3/EC2 across regions can tack 10%–20% onto your ML bill.

3. The 2026 Decision Playbook

  • Prototyping & LoRA Fine-Tuning: Use RunPod or Lambda Labs for single-to-8-GPU simplicity.
  • Multi-Node Pretraining: Use CoreWeave on committed contracts (targeting 40%–60% below list) or Lambda clusters where InfiniBand fabric matters most.
  • Regulated Enterprise Pipelines: Stay on AWS only when compliance, data gravity, or Spot/EDP discounts offset the steep on-demand markup.
